description: We are a team of data engineers & scientists presenting our CODE-ESI club of School of Information Sciences (ESI) in this Nasa hackathon
summary:
SaddSAR is an open-source web GIS that uses radar to monitor the water stored in lakes and reservoirs every month, through clouds, day and night. For each water body it maps the water surface from NASA-ISRO NISAR (L-band) and Sentinel-1 (C-band) radar, compares it with its 2015–2024 normal for that month, gives it a status from "above normal" to "severe drought", and publishes everything on an interactive map in English, French and Arabic.

Our goal is global water monitoring; our working prototype covers Morocco, which is just coming out of a severe multi-year drought. We track its 10 largest dams plus Mohamed V with a 12-year radar record. In October 2026 the dams with a long-term baseline held 116.3% of their normal water area, up from 54.5% in March 2024, while Al Mansour Ad Dahbi in the arid south is still in drought. The method runs on any lake outline, so it scales to the world's lakes and reservoirs.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Reservoirs and lakes hold the water that cities, farms and ecosystems depend on, and their storage can change dramatically within a few years. Yet most of the world's lakes and reservoirs publish no timely storage data (HydroLAKES alone maps about 1.4 million lakes larger than 10 hectares). Optical satellites can't see through clouds in the rainy season, exactly when reservoirs refill, and raw radar data is hard for non-specialists to use.

SaddSAR turns radar into four simple answers for every water body: how much surface water it holds this month; whether that is above, near or below normal for this time of year; whether it is rising or falling; and where water stress is concentrated.

HOW IT WORKS

A Python pipeline (10 steps, one command) does the following:

1. Catalog: 316 Moroccan water bodies, with outlines traced from JRC Global Surface Water's maximum water extent and OpenStreetMap, stable IDs, analysis zones and HydroBASINS river basins.

2. NISAR: we search NISAR L2 GCOV scenes with asf_search and read only the window around each reservoir from the remote file, so no full scene is downloaded.

3. Sentinel-1 baseline: 2015 to 2026, terrain-corrected RTC data from Microsoft Planetary Computer, one consistent orbit per reservoir.

4. Water detection, one algorithm shared by both sensors: speckle filter, automatic Otsu threshold (calm water looks dark), masks for the maximum water extent and for terrain more than 15 m above the reservoir, removal of small isolated patches, and a monthly majority vote across scenes.

5. Status: a per-month normal from 2015–2024 gives percent of normal, a z-score, six status classes, and month-on-month and year-on-year change. NISAR is calibrated onto the Sentinel-1 baseline.

6. Context: CHIRPS rainfall anomalies per basin separate climate (rain deficit) from human effects (irrigation, dam releases).

7. Validation against cloud-free Sentinel-2 images.

8. A static web map (MapLibre GL) with a monthly time slider, before/after swipe, time-series charts, a guided story, search and filters, alerts and data downloads, in English, French and Arabic (right-to-left).

WHAT REAL DATA TAUGHT US

- At L-band (NISAR), an exposed, dry lake bed looks almost as dark as water. Our first NISAR map of Al Massira counted 128.7 km² of water against 72 km² from Sentinel-1; re-tuning the thresholds brought it to 76–80 km².

- Wind-roughened lakes turn bright: on windy days Al Wahda looked empty while it was nearly full. We re-detect those scenes with the cross-polarised VH channel and flag implausible one-month drops.

- Reservoirs filled after 2015 have no meaningful "normal"; they are flagged instead of showing absurd percentages.

RESULTS (PROTOTYPE, MOROCCO)

- Al Massira, Morocco's second-largest dam: about 123 km² of water in 2015, 0.05 km² in June 2024, and 68.6 km² in October 2026 (146% of normal).

- The 9 dams with a long-term baseline hold 357.6 km² in October 2026, 116.3% of normal, up from 54.5% in March 2024.

- October 2026 status: 5 above normal, 2 normal, 1 on watch (Mohamed V), 1 in drought (Al Mansour Ad Dahbi), 2 new dams with no baseline yet.

- Rainfall in the 12 months to September 2026 was 37% to 81% above normal in 9 of 10 basins.

- Accuracy: radar water maps match cloud-free Sentinel-2 at a mean IoU of 0.88 (10 comparisons on 5 dams; target 0.80). NISAR and Sentinel-1 differ by about 15% for the same month (target 10%), so NISAR is scaled to Sentinel-1.

BENEFITS

Works through clouds, day and night, with a monthly cadence. Needs no ground data, so it covers reservoirs that publish nothing. Readable by the public, journalists and water managers. Open source, a static website, free data; the Sentinel-1 baseline needs no account at all.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE

Global water monitoring. The algorithm runs per lake outline and every input is already global (NISAR, Sentinel-1, JRC, Copernicus DEM, HydroBASINS, CHIRPS), so scaling up needs compute, not new science. Next: official fill rates to convert area into % full; then North Africa and the Mediterranean, updated with every 12-day NISAR pass; then every Global Dam Watch reservoir and HydroLAKES lake, with a public API, status alerts and SWOT water heights for volume.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

Python (numpy, scipy, scikit-image, rasterio, h5py, xarray, geopandas, shapely, pyproj, pandas, matplotlib, asf_search, earthaccess, pystac-client, planetary-computer, earthengine-api, pytest); JavaScript (Vite, MapLibre GL JS, maplibre-gl-compare, Chart.js); Vercel and GitHub Actions (tests, deployment, monthly data update); NASA Earthdata/ASF and Microsoft Planetary Computer for data access.
